summary.text: Apoptosis is a form of programmed cell death that occurs in multicellular organisms and in some single-celled eukaryotes such as yeast.
Unlike necrosis, which follows acute injury, it is a highly regulated and controlled process that gives an organism advantages during its life cycle.
Both of its pathways kill the cell by activating caspases, which are enzymes that degrade proteins.

facts.label: Two pathways
facts.value: Intrinsic, from cell stress, and extrinsic, from other cells' signals

facts.label: Embryo example
facts.value: Cells between developing fingers and toes die by apoptosis

facts.label: Name suggested by
facts.value: James Cormack, a professor of Greek

facts.label: 2002 Nobel Prize
facts.value: Awarded for identifying genes that control apoptosis

items.prompt: In a developing human embryo, the fingers and toes end up separate. What makes that happen?

options.label: Cells between the digits multiply until the digits are pushed apart
Cells between the digits die from sudden injury, as in necrosis
The digits grow faster than the cells that surround them
Cells between the digits die in a genetically determined process

items.explain: The separation of fingers and toes happens because cells between the digits undergo a genetically determined form of apoptosis.

items.prompt: When a cell dies by apoptosis, why don't its contents harm the cells around it?

options.label: The cell dissolves completely before it touches anything
It breaks into fragments that phagocytes engulf and remove
Neighbouring cells block the contents with their membranes
The contents are neutralized by caspases after they spill out

items.explain: Apoptosis produces cell fragments called apoptotic bodies that phagocytes engulf and remove before the contents can spill onto surrounding cells.

items.prompt: In a tissue, cells that should die by apoptosis keep surviving. Which problem is linked to too little apoptosis?

options.label: Uncontrolled cell growth, such as in cancer
Atrophy, the shrinking of tissue
Sudden traumatic cell death after an injury
Faster separation of the fingers in an embryo

items.explain: An insufficient amount of apoptosis results in uncontrolled cell proliferation, such as cancer, while excessive apoptosis causes atrophy.

items.prompt: A cell decides to die because it senses trouble within itself, not because a neighbour told it to. Which pathway of apoptosis is this?

options.label: The extrinsic pathway, started by signals from other cells
The necrotic pathway, started by traumatic injury
The intrinsic pathway, started by the cell's own stress
The executioner pathway, started by caspases alone

items.explain: In the intrinsic pathway the cell kills itself because it senses cell stress, while in the extrinsic pathway it responds to signals from other cells.

items.prompt: Why do cells keep the start of apoptosis under such tight control?

options.label: Because it can be reversed easily if the signal fades
Because it only ever affects a few cells in the body
Because it speeds up the cell cycle while it is active
Because once begun, it inevitably ends in the cell's death

items.explain: Apoptosis cannot stop once it has begun and inevitably leads to the death of the cell, so its initiation is tightly regulated.

items.prompt: In the last step of apoptosis, how do executioner caspases kill the cell?

options.label: By blocking the Bcl-2 proteins that protect the nucleus
By degrading proteins throughout the cell indiscriminately
By swelling the cell until its membrane bursts open
By switching on the Fas receptors on its surface

items.explain: Initiator caspases activate executioner caspases, which kill the cell by degrading proteins indiscriminately.
